title: Some convergence properties of the conjugate gradient method
contribution: Stronger negative result: on a convex quadratic with an arbitrary downhill initial direction, CG either terminates or converges only linearly (the usual case); necessary and sufficient start/direction relations for termination are studied (abstract).
problem_entry: Conjecture that CG converges superlinearly, already refuted by a Crowder–Wolfe example (abstract).
key_idea: Upgrade a single counterexample into a theorem over all downhill initial directions on convex quadratics (abstract); proofs not read.
assumptions: Convex quadratic objective; arbitrary downhill initial search direction (abstract).
positioning: Crowder and Wolfe's counterexample to the superlinear-rate conjecture (abstract).

method_links.method: negative result first, then relax the design parameter
method_links.note: 1976 negative rate result precedes the 1977 adaptive-restart paper S006 (link rests on the two abstracts)
conjecture is someone else's and already refuted by example; Powell generalizes the example into a theorem

transferable: When a conjecture has been refuted by one example, prove the general version (bad behaviour for every start in a natural class unless a stated condition holds), then study the exceptional set via necessary and sufficient conditions (abstract).

quotes.text: It has been conjectured that the conjugate gradient method for minimizing functions of several variables has a superlinear rate of convergence, but Crowder and Wolfe show by example that the conjecture is false.

Now the stronger result is given that, if the objective function is a convex quadratic and if the initial search direction is an arbitrary downhill direction, then either termination occurs or the rate of convergence is only linear, the second possibility being more usual.

title: Restart procedures for the conjugate gradient method
contribution: CG algorithm whose restart procedure adapts to the objective function automatically, plus reasons for one choice of the search-direction multiplying factor, supported by numerical examples (abstract).
problem_entry: CG needs no stored matrices but is only linearly convergent unless restarted; the usual fixed restart every n or n+1 iterations ignores the objective function (abstract).
key_idea: Replace the fixed restart period by an objective-dependent automatic restart test; argue for one expression of the multiplying factor (abstract); restart test not read.
experiments: Several numerical examples reported in support (abstract); scope not read.
positioning: Against the usual practice of restarting every n or (n+1) iterations (abstract).

method_links.note: keeps storage-free CG, removes one limitation: the fixed, problem-independent restart period (outside DFO)
no matrix storage is the stated reason for using CG
weak: numerical examples support the conclusions

method_links.method: negative result first, then relax the design parameter
method_links.note: follows the 1976 negative rate result S051

transferable: Replace a schedule parameter fixed by convention (restart every n iterations) by a test on quantities the iteration already computes (abstract, idea level only).

quotes.text: At present it is usual to restart every n or (n + 1) iterations, where n is the number of variables, but it is known that the frequency of restarts should depend on the objective function.
Therefore the main purpose of this paper is to provide an algorithm with a restart procedure that takes account of the objective function automatically.

problem_entry: Davidon's new variable metric algorithm terminates on quadratics without line searches (abstract).
key_idea: Re-prove a known termination property elementarily and read design freedom off the proof (abstract); proof not read.
assumptions: Positive definite second-derivative approximations; quadratic objective (abstract).
positioning: Davidon's algorithm [1] (abstract).

quotes.text: We give a new and elementary proof of these termination properties.
It shows the great freedom allowed by the algorithm in the choice of search directions and it explains the effect of a restart procedure.

A particular method is recommended that seems to be more powerful than the author believed to be possible at the beginning of 1976.

title: On the estimation of sparse Hessian matrices
contribution: Two cheap algorithms (a direct and a substitution method) that estimate a sparse Hessian from gradient differences using sparsity and symmetry to reduce the number of gradient evaluations; examples show they may not minimize that number (abstract).
problem_entry: Automatic estimation of second derivatives from first-derivative differences when the Hessian's sparsity structure is known (abstract).
key_idea: Exploit symmetry as well as sparsity to make the number of gradient vectors small (abstract); algorithms not read.
assumptions: Known sparsity structure; symmetric Hessian; gradients available (abstract).
experiments: Algorithms seem very successful in practice; examples where they are not optimal (abstract).
positioning: Extension to symmetric matrices of Curtis–Powell–Reid sparse Jacobian estimation; first of three Toint-project contributions (R007 p. 15).
limits_future: May not minimize the number of first-derivative vector calculations (abstract).

method_links.note: economy of derivative information via known structure rather than least-change updating

non-optimality examples stated in the abstract

transferable: When proposing a heuristic for a combinatorial saving (here the number of gradient differences), include examples where it is not optimal and say so in the abstract (abstract).

quotes.text: Our main purpose is to find ways of taking advantage of the sparsity structure and the symmetry of the second derivative matrix, in order to make small the number of first derivative vectors that have to be calculated.
Some examples show, however, that the given methods may not minimize the number of first derivative vector calculations.

quotes.text: The general theory of the subject and its application to polynomial approximation are classical, but piecewise polynomials have become far more useful during the last twenty years.
This book gives a thorough and coherent introduction to the theory that is the basis of current approximation methods.

title: On a decomposition of conditionally positive-semidefinite matrices
contribution: Characterization of the matrices A for which a nonnegative quadratic form on {Ax ≥ 0} always admits a decomposition Q = AᵀCA + S with C copositive and S positive semidefinite (abstract).

quotes.text: A symmetric matrix C is said to be copositive if its associated quadratic form is nonnegative on the positive orthant.
In this paper we give a characterization of those matrices A for which such a decomposition is always possible.

contribution: Watchdog technique: an extension to line-search optimization algorithms that lets some iterations take much longer steps than the line-search objective allows, with global and Q-superlinear convergence properties proved (abstract).
